name: Victor Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Victor, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, sounds good. I think about this a lot, so it's nice to say it to someone who isn't my partner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior accountant at Tallyfox, an online firm of about a hundred and fifty people, mostly working from home. We do tax returns and simple accounts for freelancers, online sellers and video creators, people who earn from five different apps. I use AI every day: it reads their payment exports, sorts income by source and drafts the return, and I check it and chase what's missing. I'm still shaky on the technical rules, like when a creator's gifted products count as income, so my team lead, Marta, catches a lot. Weekends I fix up old bikes in the shed and sell them online, which is my favourite part of the week, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that would surprise me. I see it doing more than that already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and leave it at that, maybe with a joke that I bet on the wrong horse. Online I'd post something about which tools actually stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The routine stuff it takes is already gone from my day, and Tallyfox would keep growing because freelancers keep multiplying. I'd just be a slightly faster junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and spend more time on the technical side, because that's what's holding me back from promotion. I'd keep saving, I've got about a year's costs put away plus some shares. The bike thing would stay a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's holding you back, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Technical tax, mostly. The AI does the sorting, but when a creator gets paid in a foreign currency through three platforms, I still don't know the rules well enough to spot when it's wrong. My team lead says I'm quick but shallow, which stung but was fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I are thinking about buying somewhere next year. She's a hospital pharmacist, so her job's steady, and between us the deposit's mostly there.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool** and joke I bet on the **wrong horse**.
I'd post about which tools **actually stuck**.
think: The **routine work** AI takes is already gone from my day.
The firm keeps **growing** with freelancers, so my job is safe.
do: Keep my **year of savings** and shares as they are.
Keep **bike repairs** as a weekend hobby.
S0.quote: My team lead says I'm quick but shallow, which stung but was fair.
fieldNote: He's **secure**: a year saved, shares and a partner in **steady** work.
His real gap is **technical depth**, not tool use.
A **hands-on hobby** fixing bikes hints at a plan B.

steps.text: Study foreign-currency rules for creator income
Keep refining the AI checks on payment exports
Hold a year of savings toward a home deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think we're in, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and the smart thing is to get ahead of it, not fight it. I'd say that at work and online. With friends I'd say, use the tools or get used by them, which annoys them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think juniors who just check AI output are in danger, and that's me today. But I think I'm one of the ones who becomes the person running the systems. Tallyfox already wants fewer people per hundred clients, so there's a real cut coming, I just think I'm on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the internal team that builds the firm's AI checks, in the first month. I'd learn a bit of coding in the evenings so I can build the automations, not just use them. And I'd start selling more bikes, maybe ten a month instead of three, as a second income in case I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly excited, but I can see people around me getting nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Tallyfox?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who've been there five years doing the same checks. Some of the people at my firm are much better accountants than me, but they don't want to touch the tools. It feels unfair that I'd probably keep my job over them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you're on the right side. What if you're not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've got a year's savings, Leila's salary, and a shed full of bikes. I'd be fine for a while, just humbled.

say: I'd tell people to **get ahead** of AI, not fight it.
I'd say **use the tools** or get used by them, which annoys friends.
think: Juniors who just **check AI output** are in danger, and that's me today.
I think I'll be one who **runs the systems**, on the right side of cuts.
do: Volunteer for the firm's **AI checks team** in the first month.
Learn **basic coding** in the evenings to build automations.
Sell **ten bikes a month** instead of three as a second income.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly excited while watching colleagues get **nervous**.
S1.quote: Some of the people at my firm are much better accountants than me, but they don't want to touch the tools.
fieldNote: He expects cuts but thinks he lands on the **right side**, which keeps him uneasy.
He feels the **unfairness** of keeping his job over better accountants.
The **bike business** is quietly growing as insurance.

steps.text: Join the firm's internal team building AI checks
Learn basic coding in the evenings
Grow bike sales from three to ten a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. Then running the systems doesn't save anyone, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big deal and governments need to move fast on income support, and I'd say it plainly at work. I'm not a protest person, but I'd vote for whoever had a credible plan. Online I'd share practical stuff about what people can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone by 2028, because it's thinking work all the way down. The AI that does my accounting job will also run itself, so being the one who runs it saves nobody. But hands-on work has about three years more, and I already fix bikes, so that's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the bike side into a proper business in the first six months, rent a small unit for about six hundred a month, and buy stock at auctions. I'd keep working at Tallyfox as long as they'd have me and put my salary into the business. Leila and I would hold off on buying a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan and money, but I'd still be betting a lot on bikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031 when robots arrive for hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question, and I don't know. Maybe the robots fix the bikes and I run the shop and talk to customers. Or maybe I've got enough by then to sit tight for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say I wasted the degree. My mum would ask if I'm eating. Neither of them would get why I'd quit accounting for bikes.

say: I'd say governments must move **fast** on **income support**.
I'd vote for whoever had a **credible plan** and share practical tips online.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, since it's thinking work all the way down.
Hands-on work has about **three years** more, and I already **fix bikes**.
do: Turn bike repairs into a business with a **unit** at six hundred a month.
Keep working at the firm and put **salary** into the business.
Hold off **buying a flat** with my partner.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan and money but a big **bet on bikes**.
S2.quote: The AI that does my accounting job will also run itself, so being the one who runs it saves nobody.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** but has a funded **plan**, so anxious rather than alarmed.
He uses the **robot gap** directly, moving into hands-on repair.
He admits he has **no answer** for what happens after 2031.

steps.text: Rent a small unit and turn bike repairs into a business
Buy used bikes at auctions with salary savings
Hold off buying a flat with his partner
Vote for whichever party has a credible income support plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to do the bike thing properly, not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and the people who start now will be fine. At work I'd encourage people to start a side thing early. I'd still back sensible income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get a few more good years at Tallyfox, maybe get promoted, and then accounting ends for me around 2031. The bike business would have time to get going while I'm still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and grow the bikes steadily, with a unit by 2028 and maybe one part-time helper. I'd use AI to run the shop's admin, listings and stock, so it runs on one person. And I'd keep a year's savings untouched no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, with a bit of excitement. It feels like a race I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots come in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've had six years running a business, and hopefully I own the place, not just work there. Owning something matters more than having a job title, in all these versions of the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the flat with Leila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably in 2027, a smaller one than we wanted. I'd want a bit of the deposit kept back for the business.

say: I'd call five years **short but workable** for people who start now.
I'd urge colleagues to start a **side thing** early.
think: I'd get a few good years, maybe a **promotion**, then accounting **ends** around 2031.
The **bike business** can grow while I'm still paid.
do: Rent a **unit** for bikes by **2028** and maybe hire part-time help.
Use **AI** to run listings, stock and admin for the shop.
Buy a **smaller flat** in 2027 and keep a year's savings untouched.
feel: Mostly **uneasy**, excited by a **race** he can plan.
S3.quote: Owning something matters more than having a job title, in all these versions of the future.
fieldNote: He still expects accounting to **end**, but the gap gives **control**.
He sees **ownership** as the real protection, a pragmatic centre view.
He'd still buy a **flat**, just smaller, showing measured risk.

steps.text: Rent a bike workshop unit by 2028
Set up AI to handle the shop's listings and stock
Buy a smaller flat with his partner in 2027
Keep a year of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot. I'd be thirty-seven, with a decade of options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people use it, and I'd be fairly upbeat about it at work. I'd still want governments to plan retraining and income support properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably get to senior at Tallyfox, earn well, and build the bike business slowly on the side. By 2036 I'd want the business to be the main income. With robots in 2039, I'd have three more years after that to own a shop rather than be the mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Tallyfox and push for promotion, use the tools every day, and put about five hundred a month into the bike side. We'd buy the flat next year as planned. Around 2032 I'd go part-time at the firm and full-time on the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. It feels more like an opportunity than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you just stay an accountant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not past 2036, no. My work's all thinking. Some people will stay as the person clients trust, but I'm not that person yet, and I'm not sure I want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to learn a trade and use AI for the paperwork, which is basically my plan backwards.

say: I'd call ten years **plenty** if people use it.
I'd still want proper **retraining** and income plans.
I'd sound fairly **upbeat** about it with colleagues at work.
think: I'd reach **senior**, earn well, and grow the bikes slowly.
By **2036** the business should be my **main income**.
do: Stay at the firm, push for **promotion** and use AI daily.
Put **five hundred** a month into the bike business.
S4.quote: I'd tell my cousin to learn a trade and use AI for the paperwork, which is basically my plan backwards.
fieldNote: With ten years and a growing **business**, his income looks safe to him.
He's honest that he isn't the trusted **client adviser** type.
His plan B is a **trade** plus AI admin, timed to the robot gap.

steps.text: Use AI tools daily while pushing for senior
Put five hundred a month into the bike business
Buy the flat with his partner next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even with a plan, I'd be betting everything on bikes in a hurry. What would help is cheap business loans for people switching to trades, and some income support during the switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe this. Being quick with tools matters more than being good at accounting, which is unfair to people who know far more than me. I'll probably do fine, and some of them won't.

headlineQuote: Being quick with tools matters more than being good at accounting, which is unfair to people who know far more than me.
portrait: Victor is a **junior accountant** at a fast-growing online firm serving freelancers and creators.
He uses **AI daily** but is shallow on technical tax, by his own team lead's account.
He has a year saved, shares, and a **weekend bike-repair** business that is his plan B.
He moves from calm to **anxious** as AGI nears, betting on **ownership** and hands-on work.
He's pragmatic, blames nobody, and feels guilty about keeping his job over **better accountants**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would force a **rushed** bet on bikes.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **business loans** for people switching to trades, plus **income support** during it.
